questions.scenario: Your school abruptly announces an unfair 30% fee hike. How do you react?

options.text: Start a signature campaign and lead a student strike in the playground during recess.
Read the state education board guidelines online to see if this sudden hike is actually legal.
Make a hard-hitting Instagram reel showing how this hike will force some students to change schools.
Coordinate a meeting between the PTA (Parent-Teacher Association) and the Principal to negotiate a middle ground.

questions.scenario: You notice 'Chotu', a young 10-year-old boy, washing glasses at the local tapri (tea stall) every morning. What's your approach?

options.text: Confront the stall owner directly and loudly demand that he let the kid go to school.
Look up the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act to know the exact legal penalty for the owner.
Take a poignant photograph of the boy looking at school kids and post it with a strong caption to raise awareness.
Contact a local NGO like Bachpan Bachao Andolan to ensure the child gets rescued and properly rehabilitated.

questions.scenario: The domestic helper (maid) in your society is unfairly denied leave for Diwali by the RWA (Resident Welfare Association).

options.text: Rally the other society kids and protest outside the secretary's office until they change their mind.
Check the society bylaws and RWA rules to find a loophole that guarantees her right to take a holiday.
Write a heartfelt school magazine article about the invisible, unappreciated struggles of domestic workers in India.
Talk to the RWA president logically, proposing a formal, society-wide leave policy for all helpers.

questions.scenario: Your school restricts girls from playing football on the main sports ground, saying it's 'only for boys'.

options.text: March onto the ground with all the girls and refuse to leave until the sports teacher lets you play.
Find the school's 'equality policy' in the diary and draft a formal, evidence-backed complaint.
Make a viral short film highlighting the gender bias in sports at your school.
Form a sports committee, gather support from teachers, and present a structured ground-sharing schedule to the management.

questions.scenario: Stray dogs in your colony are being cruelly chased away and beaten by the night watchmen.

options.text: Physically step in, shout at the watchmen to stop, and form a protective human chain around the dogs.
Quote the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act to the society committee to prove this is a punishable offense.
Create an awareness poster campaign showcasing the dogs' friendly nature and stick them in all the lifts.
Organize an official society meeting with an animal rescue NGO and the managing committee for a permanent, peaceful solution.

questions.scenario: A classmate is being severely bullied for their regional accent or background.

options.text: Loudly call out the bullies in the middle of the classroom and stand firmly by the victim's side.
Secretly document the bullying incidents with dates and times to present an undeniable case to the coordinator.
Direct a powerful skit for the morning assembly focusing on unity in diversity and the deep pain of exclusion.
Pitch an 'Anti-Bullying Squad' idea to the principal, outlining how prefects can monitor and report incidents effectively.

questions.scenario: Your local park is being destroyed by builders to construct a shopping mall.

options.text: Organize a 'Chipko' style protest, physically hugging the trees so the bulldozers can't cut them down.
File an RTI (Right to Information) application to check if the builder actually has the proper environmental clearances.
Shoot a documentary interviewing the senior citizens and kids who will lose their only green space.
Run a crowdfunding campaign to hire an environmental lawyer to file a PIL (Public Interest Litigation) in the High Court.

questions.scenario: During Civics class, the teacher skips the chapter on 'Fundamental Rights' to save time.

options.text: Interrupt and demand that the chapter be taught because knowing our rights is crucial for every citizen.
Go home, read the entire chapter yourself, and cross-reference it with recent news articles about freedom of speech.
Draw a cool comic strip summarizing the fundamental rights and pass it around the classroom for everyone to read.
Suggest the teacher host a 'Mock Parliament' session so the topic is covered in a fun, time-saving, and organized way.

questions.scenario: You see news about the sudden, unfair eviction of street vendors (thelawalas) in your city.

options.text: Join the street vendors in a dharna (sit-in protest) outside the municipal corporation office.
Research the Street Vendors Act of 2014 to understand if the municipality's actions are actually illegal.
Do a photo essay capturing the hard work of the vendors and share it on Twitter/X to gain public sympathy.
Connect the vendors' union with a pro-bono legal aid clinic that can officially fight their case in court.

questions.scenario: Your school is organizing a massive charity and relief drive for flood victims.

options.text: Go door-to-door in your neighborhood, loudly motivating people to donate rice, dal, and old clothes.
Calculate exactly how much relief material is needed per family and find the most efficient transport routes to the flood zones.
Make an emotional appeal video showing the devastation to urge your schoolmates to donate generously.
Partner with local businesses, manage the volunteers, and ensure the collected funds are officially audited and tracked.

Grassroots_Activist.title: The Fearless Voice (Grassroots Activist / Protest Leader)
Grassroots_Activist.primary_match_text: You are a natural-born fighter for justice! You don't sit back when you see something wrong; you take immediate, on-the-ground action. You are brave, passionate, and people naturally follow your lead.
Grassroots_Activist.day_in_the_life: Organizing massive public rallies, raising slogans for marginalized communities, speaking to the media on the streets, and directly confronting authorities to demand immediate change.
Grassroots_Activist.alternative_match_text: Your passion for public action would also make you a brilliant Politician, Social Worker, or Union Leader.
Grassroots_Activist.roadmap: 11th/12th: Humanities (Arts) with Political Science and Sociology. Degree: B.A. in Social Sciences or Political Science. Next Steps: Pursue a Master of Social Work (MSW) and intern heavily with grassroots NGOs.

Human_Rights_Researcher.title: The Truth Seeker (Human Rights Researcher / Legal Analyst)
Human_Rights_Researcher.primary_match_text: You believe that knowledge is power. You are deeply analytical, love reading the fine print, and fighting injustice by finding the exact legal loopholes. You trust facts over emotions.
Human_Rights_Researcher.day_in_the_life: Poring over thick law books, investigating human rights abuses, drafting PILs (Public Interest Litigations), and finding the undeniable evidence needed to win massive court cases.
Human_Rights_Researcher.alternative_match_text: Your analytical brain makes you a perfect fit for Investigative Journalism, Policy Analysis, or Corporate Law.
Human_Rights_Researcher.roadmap: 11th/12th: Humanities or Commerce. Entrance: Crack the CLAT (Common Law Admission Test) or AILET. Degree: 5-year B.A. LL.B (Hons.). Next Steps: Pursue an LL.M in Human Rights Law.

Social_Justice_Storyteller.title: The Empathy Creator (Social Justice Storyteller / Filmmaker)
Social_Justice_Storyteller.primary_match_text: You fight for human rights through art and emotion. You know that to change the system, you first have to change people's hearts. You are highly creative, visual, and empathetic.
Social_Justice_Storyteller.day_in_the_life: Traveling to remote villages with a camera, interviewing survivors of injustice, editing hard-hitting documentaries, and writing viral articles that shift public opinion.
Social_Justice_Storyteller.alternative_match_text: If not human rights, your creative flair would make you a brilliant Photojournalist, Creative Director, or Author.
Social_Justice_Storyteller.roadmap: 11th/12th: Any stream (Humanities preferred). Degree: B.A. in Journalism and Mass Communication (BJMC) or Bachelor of Design (B.Des). Next Steps: Specialize in Documentary Filmmaking or Visual Arts.

Legal_Aid_Director.title: The System Changer (Legal Aid Campaign Director)
Legal_Aid_Director.primary_match_text: You are a master strategist. You want to help people, but you know that real change requires money, organization, and smart management. You are the boss who makes the charity work actually happen.
Legal_Aid_Director.day_in_the_life: Managing a huge team of lawyers, pitching for funding from international bodies like the UN, networking with top judges, and directing city-wide legal awareness campaigns.
Legal_Aid_Director.alternative_match_text: Your leadership and management skills would make you an excellent NGO Founder, Public Policy Manager, or CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) Head.
Legal_Aid_Director.roadmap: 11th/12th: Any stream. Entrance: Crack CLAT for B.A. LL.B or pursue a BBA/B.A. Next Steps: Gain field experience, then crack exams for a Master of Public Policy (MPP) or an MBA in NGO Management.
